text: When is `==` the right comparison for reference types?
choices: Whenever both operands are known to be non-null, since `equals` then adds no value.
When the class does not override `equals`, since the two are then equivalent.
Never — `equals` is always correct for references and `==` only for primitives.
When you genuinely mean identity: checking against null, comparing enum constants, or asking whether two references are the same object.
explanation: The last distractor is true and useless as a rule, since you would have to check every class. The legitimate cases are narrow and worth memorising: `x == null`, enum constants (which are singletons, so identity *is* equality), and deliberate identity checks such as the first line of a well-written `equals`. Everything else is `equals`.
